notes:
I found useful material for every verse, but there are gaps. For section 2 I found real disagreements between commentators, but only a few that follow church lines. I found no Lutheran, Anglican or Assemblies of God material, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter, so those are left out. The Enduring Word page I read was cut off after v. 10, so it is only cited up to there.

# Jonah 1: Research notes

**v. 1**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the opening "Now" doesn't mean the book is a fragment of a longer work. It identifies Jonah the son of Amittai with the prophet of 2 Kings 14:25. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
- Utley (bible.org) says the Hebrew prefix on the first verb is "a textual marker for historical narrative," which hints that the author wanted the book read as history. The names Jonah ("dove") and Amittai are rare and appear together only once elsewhere, in 2 Kings 14:25, and Utley sees this as evidence the book is historical. https://bible.org/seriespage/jonah-1
- Matthew Henry says that God's word, unlike human words, is a real thing; "men's words are but wind, but God's words are substance." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_001.cfm

**v. 2**
- Guzik says Nineveh was the capital of Assyria and not an Israelite city. God was sending Jonah to a pagan, Gentile city to call it to repent. Nineveh's sin had reached the point where it called for God's specific warning. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-1/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Assyria already dominated the region, so Jonah knew well what his own country could expect from this people. "Come up before me" means the wickedness cries out for punishment, as in Genesis 4:10 and 18:20–21. Following Pusey, it takes "wickedness" to mean their harm done to others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
- Utley points out that the word "great" is used again and again in the book. He suggests this overuse might mark the story as deliberately exaggerated. He also traces the word "evil" through the book: by chapter 4 it lands on the prophet himself, which he calls an ironic reversal. https://bible.org/seriespage/jonah-1

**v. 3**
- **Tarshish:** The Pulpit Commentary says it was probably Tartessus in Spain: sent to the far east, he flees to the distant west. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm Utley adds that some evidence points to Sardinia, and the name may be a figure of speech for the ends of the earth. https://bible.org/seriespage/jonah-1
- **Why Jonah ran (views differ):**
  - Guzik gives two reasons: the danger of the job, and that Jonah didn't want Nineveh to escape judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-1/
  - The Pulpit Commentary blames national prejudice and Jonah's fear, stated in 4:2, that God would show mercy and his warning would be discredited. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
  - Ligonier (Reformed) says he disobeyed not for lack of information or under pressure; "He simply didn't want to obey." https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/3-things-jonah
- **"From the presence of the LORD":** The Pulpit Commentary gives two readings: leaving God's special presence in the Holy Land, or giving up his service as a prophet. It prefers the first. It notes the medieval Jewish scholar Kimchi's view that Jonah thought prophecy didn't reach beyond Israel, but says Jonah could never have thought he could escape God's all-seeing eye. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm Utley suggests Jonah may have thought the LORD was limited to the Promised Land. https://bible.org/seriespage/jonah-1
- **"Went down":** Utley notes the verb repeats in 1:3, 1:5 and 2:7 and may picture Jonah's slide into rebellion. https://bible.org/seriespage/jonah-1
- **The fare:** Guzik, quoting Spurgeon, warns against treating easy circumstances or inner impulses as God's guidance. When you run from God, you pay your own fare. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-1/ Utley says most Jewish commentators thought Jonah hired the whole ship, while the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads "his fare." https://bible.org/seriespage/jonah-1

**v. 4**
- Utley says "hurled" is the same verb later translated "cast" in vv. 5 and 15. Uniquely, the Hebrew pictures the ship as "thinking" it would break up. https://bible.org/seriespage/jonah-1
- Henry says God threw the wind out with force, and the storm was sent to bring Jonah back. It is a mercy to be called home, even by a tempest. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_001.cfm
- Barnes suggests the picture of the frightened ship is meant to make Jonah's own dullness stand out. Calvin rejects reading "the ship" as meaning the crew. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/1-4.html

**v. 5**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the crew were likely from several places, hence their many gods. The book presents the heathen "as devout and sincere according to their lights." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
- **Jonah's sleep (readings differ):**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the word means a very deep sleep. Jonah was worn out by anxiety and felt secure. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
  - Utley says it suggests spiritual callousness. Or, since the word is rare, it could mean a God-sent trance. https://bible.org/seriespage/jonah-1
  - Guzik suggests the storm inside Jonah made the outside storm seem small. Following Spurgeon, he applies the scene to "sleeping Christians." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-1/

**v. 6**
- The Pulpit Commentary says a prophet should have led the prayers; here a pagan's faith rebukes the prophet's stupor. The captain says "God" with the article in Hebrew, as if he had a dim idea of one supreme God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
- Utley notes the irony: the captain uses God's own commands from v. 2, "get up" and "call." https://bible.org/seriespage/jonah-1
- Henry praises the captain for helping a stranger's soul. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_001.cfm

**v. 7**
- The Pulpit Commentary cites Proverbs 16:33 and Jerome: Jonah was caught not by the power of heathen lots but by God, who guided them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
- Clarke (Methodist) says plainly that God directed the lot. Calvin says the decision to cast lots shows this was no ordinary storm. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/1-7.html
- Guzik says we can't be sure whether the sailors had spiritual insight or "an accidentally correct superstition." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-1/

**v. 8**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the sailors calmly gave Jonah every chance to clear himself or confess. They asked his occupation in case it was one that would anger the gods. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
- Henry imagines them wondering whether he was a sorcerer, or on an errand like Balaam's. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_001.cfm

**v. 9**
- Clarke says Jonah was faithful here, giving honest testimony to the God who made and rules both sea and land. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/1-9.html
- Guzik says Jonah's claim to fear the LORD was only partly true, since he was running away. He adds that Jonah may already have been repenting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-1/

**v. 10**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the sailors now grasped Jehovah's greatness, and renders their question "What is this that thou hast done?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
- TGC (Sklar) notes "the pagan sailors rebuke the Israelite prophet." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/jonah/
- Henry compares this to Abimelech rebuking Abraham. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_001.cfm

**v. 11**
- Barnes pictures the sea as if alive, obeying its Master and "demanding the runaway slave of God." Clarke notes the sailors' unusual kindness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/1-11.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says they asked Jonah, as Jehovah's prophet, how to make up for the offence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm

**v. 12: a real disagreement**
- **Jonah as penitent:**
  - Henry calls this "the language of true penitents." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_001.cfm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says Jonah, "brought to a better mind, perhaps divinely inspired," pronounces his own sentence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
  - Clarke (Methodist) sees "deep compunction" and an honest confession of sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/1-12.html
- **Jonah as stubborn:** John MacArthur's ministry (GTY, Baptist/Reformed) says repenting and heading for Nineveh would have stopped the storm. Instead Jonah stubbornly asked to be thrown overboard, in effect choosing death over his mission. https://www.gty.org/blogs/B150313/jonah-the-rogue-prophet
- **Calvin (Reformed):** Jonah was saying his death would be enough to make atonement, and his certainty came from more than the lot. Barnes says neither Jonah nor the sailors could take his life without God's command. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/1-12.html
- **Typology:** Augustine (quoted on OCA, Orthodox) compares Jonah, sacrificed for those in the storm, to Christ offered for those drowning in the world's storm. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/the-sign-of-jonah Coffman (Restoration movement, Arminian) calls this a "noble type" of the Son of God. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/jonah/4-11.html

**v. 13**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the generous sailors didn't want to carry out the sentence on a prophet. The writer keeps contrasting them with himself as a lesson for Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
- GTY says the pagans showed Jonah more compassion than he showed the Assyrians. https://www.gty.org/blogs/B150313/jonah-the-rogue-prophet
- Henry adds that the ship stayed overloaded as long as Jonah was aboard. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_001.cfm

**v. 14**
- Gill says they now prayed to the true Jehovah, not their own gods. Clarke says they prayed to Him as Maker and as the author of the storm. Calvin notes the repeated plea. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah/1-14.html
- Henry says we should be satisfied when God pleases Himself, even if He doesn't please us. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_001.cfm

**v. 15**
- The Pulpit Commentary says they lifted him "with a certain reverence." The sea "stood from its anger." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
- Henry applies it: our sin is the "Jonah" that must be thrown overboard, and God will throw our sins into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:19). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_001.cfm

**v. 16**
- **Was this real conversion?**
  - GTY calls it "reverent awe and repentant faith." https://www.gty.org/blogs/B150313/jonah-the-rogue-prophet
  - The Bible Hub study notes call their vows a genuine conversion. https://biblehub.com/jonah/1-16.htm
  - A Bible Hub Q&A notes that ancient sailors usually made offerings after storms, but these were made to the LORD alone. https://biblehub.com/q/Sailors_view_of_God_in_Jonah_1_16.htm
- Utley notes the pagans' fear grew with their knowledge, but Jonah's did not. https://bible.org/seriespage/jonah-1
- TGC (Sklar) points out that Jonah later makes sacrifices and vows himself (2:9), things "the pagan sailors already did in chapter 1!" https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/jonah/

**v. 17**
- **"Appointed":** The Pulpit Commentary says the fish wasn't created on the spot; God arranged for it to be there. "Three days and three nights," by Hebrew counting, means parts of three days. It adds that Christ's use of the story confirms it is history. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/1.htm
- **The fish:** GotQuestions says the Hebrew simply means "great fish," not a particular species, and holds that it really happened. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jonah-whale.html
- **Alive, or dead and raised?** A source quoted on Precept Austin says either reading is possible, but that he stayed alive is more likely. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jonah-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations
- **Type of Christ:**
  - Ligonier (Reformed) says Jonah died symbolically, since the sailors thought they were killing him, and the fish was his watery grave. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/3-things-jonah
  - Ellicott says the "three nights" don't fit exactly with Christ's time in the tomb and may just be a phrase borrowed from Jonah. https://biblehub.com/matthew/12-40.htm
- **Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says Catholics have always treated the book as fact, and Christ's words remove all doubt. "Not a single Father" is cited for the view that it is fiction. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/jonah (also at https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08497b.htm)
- **Orthodox:** OCA notes the whole of Jonah is read at the Holy Saturday Liturgy, and the Fathers treated Jonah as a type of Christ. It allows "However we may assess its 'historicity,'" and says most commentators date the book after the exile. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/the-sign-of-jonah
- **Modern critics:** A Plymouth Brethren book overview on StudyLight (Remmers) reports that many critics treat the book as allegory, parable or legend because of the fish. It answers that Jesus testified it was historical. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jonah.html
